## Abstract

Many believe that voter ignorance threatens democracy. Consequently, ambitious institutional remedies have been proposed – epistocratic suffrage exams, foot voting, devolution of decisions to the local level, new bureaucratic agencies to inform voters, and more. There are reasons to doubt such proposals will actually improve democratic governance, however. The mistake these proposals share is a failure to recognize that voter ignorance comes in many forms, and that existing remedies may target the wrong kinds of ignorance. We develop a new typology of voter ignorance and show that every existing proposal leaves certain types of ignorance unaddressed. If it is these neglected forms of ignorance that drive bad democratic outcomes, then the entire portfolio of remedies that philosophers have proposed is superfluous – they literally make no progress toward better governance. We end by briefly sketching how to think about the problem of voter ignorance going forward.

## Information

## 1. Introduction

 In modern democracies, many voters lack basic political knowledge – from the names, credentials, and policy platforms of candidates to which party controls the government and even the fundamental structure of their own political system. Such ignorance plausibly explains many of the bad decisions democracies make, prompting a range of proposals to mitigate its harmful effects. These include simple measures to make it easier for voters to acquire political information to more radical calls to remove ignorant voters from the electorate (§ 2). Such proposals are expensive, contentious, and in some cases morally dubious. They are worth pursuing only if they would actually improve democratic governance. We argue in this paper that there are compelling reasons to doubt they will.

 The problem is that voter ignorance comes in many forms, and existing remedies may target the wrong ones. The literature identifies three kinds of politically relevant ignorance: ignorance about candidates and their platforms, about the economics and social science needed to evaluate policy, and about the basic structure of government (§ 3). Various proposals aim to ameliorate one or more of these. But there is a fourth kind of ignorance – one that public choice economists have long recognized, but that philosophers have overlooked – which may do more to explain bad democratic outcomes than the other three. We call it deep legislative ignorance. It is ignorance of the intricate details of the bills, regulations, and administrative rules actually implemented by governments (§ 4).

 Which kinds of ignorance do existing remedies actually address? To answer this, we introduce a new conceptual framework (§ 5). Political knowledge, we argue, varies along two dimensions: how difficult it is to acquire and how transient it is. Mapping different kinds of political knowledge onto this framework reveals a striking result; although existing proposals can remedy other forms of voter ignorance, they do nothing to combat deep legislative ignorance specifically (§ 6).

 A troubling implication follows. If deep legislative ignorance is the primary driver of bad democratic policy – as public choice theory gives us reason to suspect – then the entire portfolio of remedies that political philosophers have proposed is superfluous (§ 7). That is, existing proposals may literally make no progress toward better democratic governance. Political philosophers who are concerned with voter ignorance may, in short, be looking in the wrong direction entirely. We end the paper by offering some rough thoughts on how to think about the problem of voter ignorance going forward.

## 2. Three solutions to voter ignorance

 Voters in modern democracies are ignorant. Ilya Somin (Reference Somin 2013: 17) summarizes the empirical literature: “the reality that most voters are often ignorant of even very basic political information is one of the better-established findings of social science. Decades of accumulated evidence reinforces this conclusion.” For example, only 19 percent of Americans can name the three branches of government, only 25 percent know the length of a Senator’s term, and only 30 percent know the substance of the Supreme Court’s landmark Roe v. Wade decision (Carpini and Keeter Reference Carpini and Keeter 1996: 70–71). Social scientists explain this ignorance by arguing that it is rational (Downs Reference Downs 1957). Being informed is costly, and the chances of changing the outcome of an election through voting are miniscule. Informing yourself so that you can vote well fails to pass a cost–benefit test; it is rational to be ignorant. Footnote 1 

 Democracy means that the people rule, but the empirical literature on voter ignorance suggests they might not be up to the task. What to do? There are a few different responses. One says voter ignorance actually is not a problem. Through a variety of different mechanisms – the Condorcet jury theorem, the Hong-Page theorem, deliberation, and so on – democracies transform ignorant votes into good policies (Schwartzberg Reference Schwartzberg 2015). Although much is compelling in this literature, we set it to the side and focus on those who believe voter ignorance is a serious problem to be addressed.

 Responses fall into three camps. First is what we call the epistocratic voting strategy, which addresses the problem of voter ignorance by either removing ignorant voters from the electorate or by keeping them in the electorate but attenuating the impact of their votes in some way. There are several ways to do this.

 The simplest is restricted suffrage (Brennan Reference Brennan 2016: 211–212; Jones Reference Jones 2020: 106). According to this proposal, all individuals are required to pass a suffrage exam or acquire some relevant education credential before they can vote. Another example is plural voting (Brennan Reference Brennan 2016: 213; Mill Reference Mill, Philp and Rosen 2015: 292–293). Everyone gets to vote, but more votes are given to those who possess political knowledge, demonstrated by passing an exam or achieving some relevant education credential. The most complicated epistocratic voting strategy is enlightened preference voting (Ahlstrom-Vij Reference Ahlstrom-Vij 2022; Brennan Reference Brennan 2016: 220–222). Using complex statistical techniques, this voting method aims to simulate how an electorate would vote were everyone fully informed. This simulation, not the actual votes cast, decides the election. Footnote 2 

 We call the second camp the voter empowerment strategy. The idea here is that we incentivize voters to inform themselves by increasing the benefits of being informed. Recall the standard explanation for voter ignorance; the costs of being informed are high, but the benefits are low. If the benefits of being informed increase, then acquiring political information may become rational.

 The most straightforward approach to voter empowerment involves providing monetary incentives to voters to pass a civics exam (Lupia Reference Lupia 2016: 174–177; Somin Reference Somin, Samaržija and Cassam 2023: 299–300). Other proposals are more involved. For instance, one prominent strategy makes it easier for people to “vote with their feet” – that is, to leave one political jurisdiction and enter another (Friedman Reference Friedman 2019: 317; Somin Reference Somin 2013: 122). The standard rational choice explanation for voter ignorance is that a single vote is unlikely to be decisive. But an individual’s decision to move jurisdictions is inherently decisive; it directly changes his/her circumstances. This ability to take decisive action increases the incentive to acquire political information, as voters can actually act on what they learn. Opportunities for foot voting can be expanded through institutional structures such as federalism and polycentricity (Somin Reference Somin 2020: 45–66) as well as economic redistribution to make relocation more affordable (Friedman Reference Friedman 2019: 334).

 A final voter empowerment strategy devolves power to the local level. Fewer voters make up the electorate in local elections, which means the probability that a single vote decides the election increases. Given the increased value of a single vote, the hope is that voters will be more willing to acquire political information to ensure they vote well. Although many of the Confucian meritocrats are skeptical of democracy, they are more sanguine about its prospects at lower levels of government (Bai Reference Bai 2020: 70–71; Bell Reference Bell 2015: 168–175). This is due (in part) to the fact that voters are more likely to be informed in local elections (Bai Reference Bai 2020: 70).

 The third and final camp we call the voter education strategy. Instead of increasing the benefits of being informed – as the voter empowerment strategy does – this approach reduces the costs. If being informed is cheap enough, voters will inform themselves, even if the benefits of doing so are not substantial.

 Marie Collins Swabey (Reference Swabey 1931) was an early advocate of this. She recommended “the development of a great national bureau of publicity,” whose job is “the collection of information on all socially important subjects and its dissemination to the country at large by means of the various scientific and artistic devices of the day” (Swabey Reference Swabey 1931: 106). The agency’s job would be to publicize important political information in easily digestible formats. In a similar vein, Giavazzi and Kapelner (Reference Giavazzi and Kapelner 2024: 728) argue that the state should do things like offer “informative classes on issues relevant to voting and public decision-making or upcoming ballots.” Footnote 3 Others advocate we pursue voter education not through a new bureaucracy or state-run classes, but with more palatable journalism (Carpini and Keeter Reference Carpini and Keeter 1996: 275; Dewey Reference Dewey 2016: 204; Lupia Reference Lupia 2016: 63).

## 3. The varieties of voter ignorance

 Voter ignorance, many worry, threatens democracy. But ignorance of what, exactly? Most voters do not know all the elements of the periodic table or the details of Kant’s epistemology, but it is hard to see how ignorance of these matters threatens democracy. Other forms of ignorance plausibly do cause problems, however. We need a precise account of what exactly voters need to know for democracy to function well.

 Jason Brennan describes one kind of knowledge that he and others (e.g., Gibbons Reference Gibbons 2021: 196; Somin Reference Somin 2013: 18) think crucial for democracy to function well:

 Knowing the answers to the easy questions is not enough to be well informed about politics. To be well informed, citizens also need to know the candidates’ policy platforms, how candid
